slides.text: During the city-wide blackout of 1978, the 7th Arrondissement of Paris was plunged into total ink. From his sixth-floor attic window, Henri, a solitary translator, looked across the narrow cobblestone alleyway into the illuminated mansard window thirty feet away. A woman was sitting by the pane with an oil lamp, playing a cello. The music was lost to the street noise below, but the graceful sweep of her bow against the strings seemed to conduct the rhythm of the falling snow.

Henri took a pocket flashlight and signaled against her glass: three rapid pulses. Across the alley, the woman paused, set down her bow, picked up a candle, and answered with three pulses of her own. For three weeks of power outages, they developed an intricate nocturnal alphabet of flashes and shadows. She would play silent sonatas by candlelight; he would translate verses of Baudelaire into rhythmic light pulses against her shutter. They never met. They never exchanged a single spoken syllable.

On the night the electric grid roared back to life, flooding the boulevard in blinding neon, Henri rushed to his window, panicked that their secret language was shattered forever. The woman’s window across the alley was dark. But as he looked down at the courtyard below, she was standing beneath the lamppost in a red wool scarf, looking up at his attic. She held no flashlight—only a handwritten sign pressed against her chest: 'I have memorized every word you shone.'
